question: In Home Alone, the McCallisters fly to Paris and forget one small detail: their son. What’s his first name?
hint: Aftershave slap, scream, repeat. His name rhymes with “Devin.”
funFact: The McCallister house is a real home in Winnetka, Illinois. No word on whether the paint cans are still on the stairs.

question: Tradition says if you get caught standing under which plant, you owe somebody a kiss? (Choose your doorways carefully.)
hint: It hangs over doorways, grows high in treetops, and causes awkward pauses.
funFact: The plant of romance is partly a parasite: it moves into a tree and steals its water and nutrients. Very romantic.

question: At Mexican Christmas parties, blindfolded kids swing a stick at a star-shaped papier-mâché figure stuffed with candy. What is it?
hint: It hangs from a rope, gets whacked by kids, and pays out in candy. Best job ever.
funFact: The classic Christmas version is a seven-pointed star, often said to stand for the seven deadly sins. Whack the sins, win candy!

question: According to the song, Frosty the Snowman has two eyes made out of coal and a nose made out of what?
hint: It’s “cute as” one. Usually found on a coat, often missing from one.
funFact: The nose isn’t the magic part: it’s the old silk hat that brings Frosty to life. Fashion really does make the snowman.

question: In A Christmas Carol, what is the name of Bob Cratchit's sickly little son?
hint: He’s small, he’s hopeful, and he says “God bless us, every one!”
funFact: Dickens published it on December 19, 1843, and the first printing sold out by Christmas Eve. Five days. No online shopping.

question: In which holiday movie do a mom, a teacher AND a store Santa all deliver the same warning: “You’ll shoot your eye out”?
hint: Ralphie wants a Red Ryder BB gun. Every grown-up in town wants him to want anything else.
funFact: The narrator is Jean Shepherd, the humorist whose stories inspired the film. He also cameos as a grumpy guy in the line to see Santa.

question: In The Nightmare Before Christmas, who is Halloween Town’s Pumpkin King, bored of scaring and suddenly VERY into Christmas?
hint: Tall, pinstriped, all bones, and owner of a glowing ghost dog named Zero.
funFact: Tim Burton dreamed it up, Henry Selick directed it, and composer Danny Elfman supplied Jack’s singing voice. Teamwork makes the scream work.

question: In Elf, what sweet stuff does Buddy pour all over his spaghetti? (Somewhere, a dentist just fainted.)
hint: It drips from trees, Vermont and Canada brag about it, and pancakes miss it.
funFact: Buddy says elves stick to four main food groups: candy, candy canes, candy corn and syrup. A balanced diet, technically.

question: What do kids hang up on Christmas Eve, hoping Santa will fill them to the brim?
hint: Hung by the chimney with care. Shaped for feet, filled with treats.
funFact: In a popular version of the St. Nicholas legend, gold he tossed in for three poor sisters landed in stockings drying by the fire. Laundry day paid off!

question: Every year a giant tree towers over the famous ice rink at which New York City landmark? (Bring skates. And patience.)
hint: Named for a family so rich their last name practically means “loaded.”
funFact: It started in 1931, when construction workers decorated a scrappy little tree with cranberries, paper garlands and even tin cans.

question: What hook-shaped, red-and-white striped peppermint treat doubles as a tree ornament?
hint: Flip it upside down and it’s the letter J. Leave it in a stocking and it’s sticky forever.
funFact: The cozy tale that a German choirmaster invented them in 1670 to keep kids quiet in church? Zero evidence. Great story, though.

question: In which animated Tom Hanks movie does a doubting boy hop aboard a magical train bound for the North Pole on Christmas Eve?
hint: All aboard! It’s a Chris Van Allsburg picture book, and the train serves hot cocoa.
funFact: Tom Hanks played several roles, including the Conductor, the hobo AND Santa. Hardest-working man on that train.

question: Finish the lyric from “Santa Claus Is Comin' to Town”: “He's making a list and…”
hint: Santa does his own fact-checking. Once is never enough.
funFact: J. Fred Coots and Haven Gillespie wrote it in 1934. Santa has been double-checking ever since.

question: What thick, creamy holiday drink is dusted with nutmeg and sometimes spiked with rum or bourbon?
hint: It shows up in the dairy aisle every December, and half its name is a breakfast food.
funFact: In 1826, whiskey smuggled in for this drink sparked West Point’s “Eggnog Riot,” and about 20 cadets were court-martialed. Worst holiday party ever.

question: Cookies are for Santa. What crunchy veggie do lots of kids leave out for the reindeer?
hint: Orange, crunchy, and a snowman’s favorite nose.
funFact: In the UK, Santa’s snack is often a mince pie and a glass of sherry instead of milk and cookies. Fancy!

question: Because of the way ice crystals form, almost every snowflake has how many arms or points?
hint: Count the legs on an ant. Snowflakes match it.
funFact: Vermont farmer Wilson “Snowflake” Bentley snapped the first photo of a single snowflake in 1885. Peak dedication, very cold fingers.

question: In How the Grinch Stole Christmas, the Grinch’s small heart grows how many sizes that day?
hint: Count the little pigs. Or the blind mice.
funFact: Dr. Seuss published the book in 1957, and it’s still the most famous heart upgrade in history.

question: According to It’s a Wonderful Life, what happens every time a bell rings?
hint: Clarence has been waiting a VERY long time for this promotion.
funFact: The 1946 film disappointed at the box office, then TV reruns turned it into a beloved classic. Comeback of the century!

question: Finish the lyric from “The Christmas Song”: “Chestnuts roasting on an open fire, Jack Frost nipping at your…”
hint: The part of your face that turns Rudolph-red in the cold.
funFact: Mel Tormé and Bob Wells wrote it on a sweltering summer day in 1945, trying to think cool thoughts. Nat King Cole made it a classic.

question: What December countdown calendar has a little door to open every day before Christmas? (Some of us peek ahead.)
hint: Named after the church season before Christmas. Bonus points if there’s chocolate inside.
funFact: Printed versions caught on in early-1900s Germany; printer Gerhard Lang often gets credit for the first. The chocolate came later. Progress!

question: Finish the carol lyric: “Deck the halls with boughs of…”
hint: A spiky evergreen with red berries. Also a popular girl’s name.
funFact: Thomas Oliphant’s original 1862 English words said “Deck the hall”: just one hall. Somebody got ambitious.

question: Which Home Improvement star startles Santa off a roof and accidentally becomes him in 1994’s The Santa Clause?
hint: He also voices Buzz Lightyear. To infinity and beyond the chimney!
funFact: Nearly 30 years later he suited up again for the Disney+ series The Santa Clauses (2022). The beard never really left.

question: What spiced dough gets built into edible houses held together by icing, candy and hope?
hint: Its star spice is a knobbly root, and one cookie made of it famously runs away.
funFact: Gingerbread houses took off in 19th-century Germany, helped along by Hansel and Gretel: a story where the candy house belongs to a witch.

question: Down Under in Australia, Christmas falls during which season?
hint: Southern Hemisphere. Pack sunscreen, not mittens.
funFact: Plenty of Aussies celebrate with a barbecue or seafood lunch and a trip to the beach. Sand-men instead of snowmen!

question: In “’Twas the Night Before Christmas,” the children were nestled all snug in their beds while visions of what danced in their heads?
hint: A fairy in The Nutcracker is named after them, and she does NOT share.
funFact: Plot twist: sugarplums usually had no plums in them. They were little sugar-coated candies. False advertising!

question: In which 1947 classic does a department-store Santa named Kris Kringle end up in court proving he’s the real deal?
hint: It’s set around Macy’s in New York, and the Post Office saves the day.
funFact: Edmund Gwenn won an Oscar for playing Kris Kringle: the rare Santa with a trophy shelf.

question: Which Christmas ballet has a girl named Clara, a toy-soldier prince and an epic battle with the Mouse King?
hint: The title star is a wooden toy with a jaw strong enough for walnuts.
funFact: It’s based on E.T.A. Hoffmann’s 1816 story “The Nutcracker and the Mouse King.” Tchaikovsky added the music everyone hums in December.

question: In Britain, Santa Claus traditionally goes by what other name? (Same guy, fancier accent.)
hint: Two words. Old pictures show him in a long green robe, like a very festive dad.
funFact: He started out as a separate English figure who stood for Christmas cheer, then merged with Santa. A very jolly merger.

question: According to the Bible, what three gifts did the Wise Men bring to baby Jesus?
hint: One is a sparkly precious metal; the other two are fragrant tree resins.
funFact: Fun twist: the Bible never says there were three wise men. Tradition counted the gifts, not the visitors.

question: In “We Wish You a Merry Christmas,” what dessert do the carolers demand before they’ll leave?
hint: A steamed British pudding whose name rhymes with “piggy.”
funFact: The carolers flat-out refuse to leave: “We won’t go until we get some!” The original pushy party guests.

question: Which TV channel’s “Countdown to Christmas” is famous for cozy movies where a big-city exec falls for a small-town baker?
hint: Its logo has a little crown, just like the greeting cards.
funFact: It began as a greeting-card business in Kansas City in 1910. Sappy, heartwarming endings? It’s in the brand DNA.

question: Which red-and-green Christmas plant has bright red “petals” that are actually leaves?
hint: Native to Mexico and named after a US diplomat.
funFact: It’s named after Joel Poinsett, the first US minister to Mexico, who brought it home in the 1820s. Best souvenir ever.

question: A “German” Christmas legend: hide this ornament deep in the tree, and whoever spots it first wins a prize. Most Germans have never heard of it! What is it?
hint: It's green, it's crunchy, and last week it lived in a jar.
funFact: In a 2016 poll, about 91% of Germans had never heard of it. Meanwhile, Berrien Springs, Michigan, was crowned the “Christmas Pickle Capital of the World.”

question: Iceland's scariest Christmas monster gobbles up anyone who didn't get new clothes for Christmas. Is it a giant cat, a giant goat or a giant troll?
hint: Purr-haps you should check your sweater for a price tag.
funFact: It's the pet of Grýla, the troll mother of the Yule Lads. The legend kept everyone working: finish your chores, earn new clothes, stay off the menu.

question: Ukrainian Christmas trees often sparkle with tiny webs. A legend says which little critter secretly decorated a poor family's bare tree overnight?
hint: Eight legs, zero decorating budget.
funFact: In the morning sun, the web shimmered like silver. The web ornaments are called pavuchky, “little spiders,” and finding a web on your tree is said to bring good luck.

question: Iceland's favorite Christmas Eve tradition: unwrap one of these, then spend the night curled up with it and some chocolate. What is it?
hint: It has a spine but no bones, and you can't stop turning its pages.
funFact: It's called Jólabókaflóð, the “Christmas Book Flood.” Every November, every home in Iceland gets a free catalog of the year's new books.

question: Before Christmas Eve dinner, some Czech and Slovak families keep a live guest swimming in the bathtub for a day or two. What is it?
hint: It's on the dinner menu, and right now it's doing laps.
funFact: Some kids name it and beg to set it free. After dinner, families tuck a scale from it into their wallets, said to keep money in there all year.

question: In Home Alone, what nickname do burglars Harry and Marv proudly give themselves?
hint: Marv floods every house they rob. It’s a soggy signature.
funFact: In Home Alone 2 they rebrand as the Sticky Bandits. Same guys, new logo.

question: In Love Actually, how does Mark silently tell Juliet he loves her on her doorstep?
hint: “Silent Night” plays from a stereo while he flips through his feelings one page at a time.
funFact: Mark is played by Andrew Lincoln, who went on to battle zombies as Rick Grimes on The Walking Dead.

question: In Christmas Vacation, instead of a cash bonus, Clark Griswold gets a membership to what?
answer: The Jelly of the Month Club
hint: Cousin Eddie calls it “the gift that keeps on giving the whole year.” Spreadable!
funFact: Clark had already put a deposit on a backyard swimming pool, counting on that bonus. Oof.

question: Which actor plays a cool, wisecracking Santa who belts out a song in a jail cell in Netflix’s The Christmas Chronicles (2018)?
hint: He starred in Tombstone and Escape from New York. Tough guy, fluffy beard.
funFact: His real-life partner, Goldie Hawn, pops up at the end as Mrs. Claus. Casting by the North Pole HR department.

question: In Gremlins, Billy gets a furry mogwai for Christmas. What’s the one thing you must never do to it after midnight?
hint: Not water, not bright light: the third rule. Hide the midnight snacks.
funFact: Gremlins was one of the films that led to the PG-13 rating in 1984. Turns out “cute pet movie” was false advertising.

question: In Die Hard (1988), John McClane fights off terrorists at a Christmas Eve office party in which fictional LA skyscraper?
hint: It’s named after the Japanese company that owns it. Worst office party ever.
funFact: In real life it’s Fox Plaza in Century City, the headquarters of 20th Century Fox. Talk about filming at the office.

question: Snow looks white, but what color is a single ice crystal of a snowflake really?
hint: Think of a freshly washed window. Or a ghost’s favorite color.
funFact: Snow looks white because zillions of crystal surfaces bounce all the sunlight back at you, the same reason crushed glass looks white.

question: Which band turned Santa’s sleigh into a souped-up hot rod in the 1963 hit “Little Saint Nick”?
hint: California surf songs, sunny harmonies, and a sleigh with a big engine.
funFact: The song brags about Santa’s sleigh like a tricked-out car: basically one of the band’s hot-rod songs, with reindeer.

question: Which former Beatle released “Happy Xmas (War Is Over)” in 1971?
hint: He also wrote “Imagine.” Imagine that.
funFact: It grew out of John and Yoko's 1969 billboard campaign: “WAR IS OVER! If You Want It.”

question: “Let It Snow! Let It Snow! Let It Snow!” was written in 1945 during what kind of weather? (Spoiler: ironic.)
hint: It was July in Hollywood. Somebody needed to think cool thoughts.
funFact: Bonus irony: the lyrics never mention Christmas at all. It’s technically just a song about the weather.

question: Marshmallows for toasting, caroling out in the snow… and what kind of stories does “It’s the Most Wonderful Time of the Year” promise?
hint: The kind you’d normally save for Halloween. Boo-letide!
funFact: Victorians loved a spooky Christmas. After all, A Christmas Carol is a ghost story with four ghosts.

question: Which Canadian crooner's 2011 album “Christmas” was so huge that memes joke he “thaws out” every November?
hint: Smooth Canadian crooner of “Haven’t Met You Yet” and “Home.” Every November, he’s back.
funFact: It was the second best-selling album of 2011 in the US, beaten only by Adele’s “21.” Not bad for a seasonal job.

question: In A Charlie Brown Christmas (1965), which character takes the stage to explain the true meaning of Christmas?
hint: He’s never without his security blanket, until that very speech.
funFact: The special won an Emmy and a Peabody Award. Not bad for a show starring a sad little tree.

question: In the very first full episode of The Simpsons (1989), the family adopts a dog on Christmas Eve. What is his name?
hint: A racing greyhound who finished dead last. Still the best present they got.
funFact: The episode, “Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire,” aired December 17, 1989. Best. Pun. Ever.

question: In The Office, which Dunder Mifflin employee dresses up as Belsnickel for a Pennsylvania Dutch Christmas?
hint: Beet farmer. Assistant (to the) Regional Manager. Bears.
funFact: Belsnickel is real folklore: a fur-clad gift-bringer from German and Pennsylvania Dutch tradition. So: impish, or admirable?

question: In which country do families pre-order a bucket of KFC for Christmas dinner, sometimes weeks in advance?
hint: Christmas Eve there is more of a date night, and the Colonel statues dress up as Santa.
funFact: It all started with KFC’s 1974 “Kentucky for Christmas” campaign. Finger-lickin’ festive!

question: In Alpine folklore, which horned, half-goat creature tags along with St. Nicholas to deal with the naughty kids?
hint: St. Nick’s scary sidekick: chains, a bundle of sticks, and zero chill.
funFact: On Krampusnacht, December 5, costumed Krampuses parade through towns in Austria and Bavaria. Be good. Seriously.

question: Rovaniemi, which calls itself the “Official Hometown of Santa Claus,” is in which country?
hint: It’s in Lapland, right on the Arctic Circle. Saunas and reindeer: check.
funFact: Its Santa Claus Village draws hundreds of thousands of visitors a year, and Santa clocks in every single day. No vacation!

question: What is the holiday on December 26 called in the UK, Canada and Australia? (No gloves required.)
hint: Big sales, big sports, and a name that sounds like a fight.
funFact: The name likely comes from “Christmas boxes” of money or gifts once given to servants and tradespeople. Zero punching involved.

question: What do Germans call the hot spiced wine sold at their Christmas markets?
hint: Comes in a souvenir mug and warms you right down to your mittens.
funFact: Its name literally means “glow wine.” Very accurate marketing.

question: What tall, dome-shaped sweet bread from Milan, studded with candied fruit, shows up in a giant box every December?
hint: Its name means “large loaf” in Italian. Taller than your average fruitcake.
funFact: Bakers cool it hanging upside down so the fluffy dome doesn’t collapse. Bread yoga!

question: Which French Christmas dessert is a rolled sponge cake dressed in chocolate “bark,” often topped with meringue mushrooms?
hint: It’s shaped like firewood, but please don’t toss it in the fireplace.
funFact: It’s a tribute to the old custom of burning a giant Yule log on the hearth. Now you just eat the log.

question: Many Italian-American families celebrate Christmas Eve with the “Feast of the Seven…” what?
hint: Meat is skipped that night, so dinner comes straight from the sea.
funFact: It grew out of the Catholic custom of skipping meat on Christmas Eve, and many families call it La Vigilia. Pass the calamari!

question: The famous Christmas Truce, when enemy soldiers sang carols and swapped gifts in no man's land, happened during which war?
hint: Soldiers faced each other from muddy trenches.
funFact: It began on Christmas Eve 1914, and some accounts describe British and German soldiers playing football (soccer) together in no man’s land.

question: When the Soviet Union brought back the banned Christmas tree in 1935, which holiday was it decorated for instead?
hint: Still Russia’s biggest winter party: fireworks, a countdown and a midnight toast.
funFact: In Russia, Ded Moroz (“Grandfather Frost”) still brings the presents at New Year, with his granddaughter Snegurochka, the Snow Maiden.

question: In 1882, Edison’s business partner Edward H. Johnson lit the first electric Christmas tree. What three colors were its 80 bulbs?
hint: Think fireworks on the Fourth of July.
funFact: Before electric lights, people clipped real lit candles onto their trees. Firefighters, please look away.

question: What natural chemical makes your peppermint treats feel cold in your mouth?
hint: It’s also in cough drops and chest rubs. Your sinuses know it well.
funFact: It tricks your cold-sensing nerves into firing, so your mouth feels chilly even though nothing got colder. Delicious lies!

question: Unlike nearly every other kind of deer, female reindeer also grow what?
hint: Bony headgear that’s shed and regrown every year. Great for hanging ornaments.
funFact: Males drop theirs after the autumn mating season, but females keep theirs all winter, so Santa’s antlered team may well be all girls.

question: What British Christmas table favorite is a paper tube two people pull until it bangs, spilling out a paper crown, a joke and a toy?
hint: Same name as the crunchy snack you put cheese on.
funFact: London confectioner Tom Smith is credited with inventing them in the 1840s: first wrapped sweets, then he added the bang. The jokes got worse from there.

question: Queen Victoria's husband helped make the Christmas tree fashionable in Britain in the 1840s. What was his name?
hint: He was born in Germany, and London’s Royal ___ Hall is named after him.
funFact: When a US magazine reprinted an 1848 picture of the royals around their tree, it erased Victoria’s tiara and Albert’s mustache. Photo editing, 1850 style!

question: Canada Post gives Santa his very own postal code. What is it?
hint: It’s a pun on his famous laugh, spelled with letters and zeros.
funFact: Santa gets about a million letters a year through Canada Post, and each one is answered in the language it was written in. Busy elves!

question: In The Elf on the Shelf, what is the one thing children must never do to the scout elf, or it could lose its magic?
hint: It involves your hands. Look all you want, but keep them in your pockets.
funFact: Carol Aebersold and her daughter Chanda Bell self-published the book in 2005. Parents have been sneaking that elf around at midnight ever since.

question: Every year the Swedish town of Gävle builds a giant straw Christmas animal, and pranksters keep trying to burn it down. What animal is it?
hint: It's got horns, a beard and a very nervous fire marshal.
funFact: The very first one, built in 1966, went up in flames on New Year's Eve. Today it has guards, fences and a live webcam, and it's still a hot target.

question: In Wales, the Mari Lwyd goes door to door at Christmastime, challenging families to a rhyming battle. It's a decorated skull of which animal, on a pole?
hint: Its relatives pull carriages and win the Kentucky Derby.
funFact: The rhyme battle is called the pwnco. If the family runs out of comebacks, the skull and its crew march right in for food and drink!

question: For decades, folks in Caracas, Venezuela, got to pre-dawn Christmas Masses in a famously fun way. How did they get there?
hint: Wheels on their feet, not under a car.
funFact: The “patinatas” took off in the 1950s, and streets were sometimes closed to cars so skaters could glide to the early-morning Masses.

question: On Christmas Eve, a single Czech woman stands with her back to the door and tosses this over her shoulder. If it points to the door, she'll marry within a year! What is it?
hint: Cinderella lost one at the ball.
funFact: Toe toward the door means wedding bells. Heel toward the door means one more year of single life, and hopping around on one foot until you fetch it.

question: NORAD tracks Santa every Christmas Eve thanks to a 1955 Sears newspaper ad that got one important detail wrong. What was misprinted?
hint: Kids dialed it hoping to reach Santa and got the military instead.
funFact: Col. Harry Shoup answered the secret line, played along and gave kids Santa's location. He became known as the “Santa Colonel.”

question: Catalan nativity scenes hide a cheeky little figure in the corner called the caganer. What is he doing back there?
hint: He really should have gone before he left the house.
funFact: Today you can buy caganers of celebrities, from soccer stars to Taylor Swift. Leaving him out of the scene is said to bring a bad year for the harvest!

question: In Japan, Christmas Eve is a night for couples: fancy dinners, light displays, gifts for two. It's basically Japan's version of which other holiday?
hint: Think roses, chocolates and a table for two.
funFact: Couples book fancy dinners weeks ahead, and there's even a word, “kuribocchi,” for spending Christmas alone.

question: When tinsel was invented in Germany centuries ago, its shiny strands were made from which precious metal?
hint: It's what you win for coming in second at the Olympics.
funFact: Fancy, but the real silver tarnished fast in candle smoke. Later makers tried other metals, and today most tinsel is plain old plastic.

question: Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer was born in 1939 as a free giveaway booklet for which department store chain?
hint: A Chicago mail-order catalog giant from 1872. Its founder’s first name is also Alabama’s capital.
funFact: Copywriter Robert L. May wrote it, and the store handed out about 2.4 million copies the first year. Most successful reindeer in marketing history.

question: In The Muppet Christmas Carol (1992), which Oscar-winning British actor plays Scrooge, totally straight, opposite a frog?
hint: He played Alfred the butler in the Dark Knight films.
funFact: It was the first Muppet movie made after Jim Henson’s death, and his son Brian directed it. Kermit, naturally, plays Bob Cratchit.

question: Count every gift in every verse of “The Twelve Days of Christmas,” repeats included (the partridge alone arrives 12 times). What's the grand total?
hint: Somewhere between 300 and 400. Your true love REALLY overdid it.
funFact: That’s one gift for every day of the year, minus one. Your true love needs a storage unit.

question: In the 1970 stop-motion special Santa Claus Is Comin' to Town, which legendary dancer narrates as the mailman?
hint: Top hat, tails, and Ginger Rogers’ most famous dance partner.
funFact: Mickey Rooney voices Kris Kringle, the young toymaker who grows up to become Santa. Santa’s origin story!

question: The “X” in “Xmas” isn’t really an English X. Which Greek letter is it?
hint: It’s the first letter of “Christ” in Greek, and it rhymes with “sky.”
funFact: The abbreviation has been used in English since the 1500s, so it isn’t a modern shortcut. It’s a very, very old shortcut.

question: In the Netherlands, Sinterklaas arrives each November by steamboat from which country? (Long commute.)
hint: Sunny, southern, and famous for flamenco and paella.
funFact: The name “Santa Claus” comes from Sinterklaas. Say it fast with a Dutch accent and you’ll hear it.

question: How many mischievous Yule Lads visit Icelandic kids, one per night, in the days before Christmas?
hint: A baker’s dozen of troublemakers.
funFact: Kids leave a shoe on the windowsill: good ones get a treat, naughty ones get a potato. A potato!

question: Every Christmas Eve at 3 p.m., millions of Swedes sit down to watch an old cartoon special starring which Disney character?
hint: Sailor shirt, no pants, and a temper you can hear through the quacks.
funFact: It has aired every Christmas Eve since 1960 and still draws around 3 million viewers in a country of about 10.5 million. Quack-tastic.

question: In Catalonia, kids “feed” a smiling object for weeks, then whack it with sticks at Christmas until it “poops” out sweets. What is it?
hint: Made of wood, wears a little red hat and a big painted smile.
funFact: It typically “poops” turrón (nougat) and other treats while the family sings a song ordering it to. Festive, and gloriously weird.

question: In Italy, which kindly old witch flies on her broomstick to bring children gifts on the eve of Epiphany?
hint: Her name comes from the Italian word for Epiphany, and she brings her own broom.
funFact: Naughty kids may get a lump of “coal,” often made of black sugar. Even the punishment is candy!

question: In December 1965, the Gemini 6A astronauts played “Jingle Bells” in orbit. One shook little bells; what did the other play?
hint: A pocket-sized instrument you blow into. Bluesy, but make it space.
funFact: Just before playing, the crew jokingly reported a UFO piloted by someone in a red suit. The Smithsonian calls them the first instruments played in space.

question: What is the proper title of the poem everybody calls “’Twas the Night Before Christmas”?
accept: Account of a Visit from St. Nicholas
hint: Five words that name the poem’s famous chimney-climbing guest.
funFact: It first ran anonymously in the Troy Sentinel in 1823. Clement Clarke Moore claimed it years later, though some say Henry Livingston Jr. wrote it. Whodunit!

question: Which New York newspaper printed the famous 1897 editorial “Yes, Virginia, there is a Santa Claus”?
hint: One short word. It also rises every morning.
funFact: Eight-year-old Virginia O’Hanlon wrote in to ask, and the reply became the most reprinted newspaper editorial in English. Legendary scoop, kid.

question: The real St. Nicholas was a 4th-century bishop of Myra. Which modern-day country is Myra in?
hint: Its biggest city straddles Europe and Asia, and it shares a name with a holiday dinner.
funFact: In 1087, sailors from Bari, Italy, made off with most of his bones, which still rest in Bari’s Basilica of San Nicola. Santa got relocated!

question: From 1659 to 1681, celebrating Christmas could cost you a five-shilling fine in which American colony?
hint: A New England colony run by Puritans; Boston was its main town.
funFact: Historians have found no record of anyone actually being prosecuted under the law. The Christmas police had a very quiet 22 years.

question: Reindeer eyes change color with the seasons: golden in summer, and what color in the dark Arctic winter?
hint: Think icy and cold. A little bit Elsa.
funFact: Scientists reported it in 2013: the shift helps them see in the near-constant winter darkness. Built-in night vision for sleigh duty!

question: In the carol “O Tannenbaum,” what kind of evergreen does “Tannenbaum” literally mean in German?
hint: Three letters. Sounds like what a cat leaves all over your sweater.
funFact: In German, “Tanne” means fir and “Baum” means tree. So you’ve basically been singing “Oh, Fir Tree” all these years.

question: Which 19th-century Harper's Weekly cartoonist drew dozens of Santa illustrations that shaped the jolly, bearded Santa we know today?
hint: His cartoons also took on New York’s crooked “Boss” Tweed.
funFact: His first Santa, in January 1863, handed out gifts to Union soldiers in a Civil War camp. Santa’s first gig: morale officer.

question: In the 1974 TV special The Year Without a Santa Claus, which character forces the feuding Snow Miser and Heat Miser to compromise?
hint: She’s their mom, and everyone blames her when the picnic gets rained out.
funFact: The bickering Misers were such breakout stars that they got their own spin-off in 2008, A Miser Brothers’ Christmas. Sibling rivalry pays!

question: Which hot spiced Christmas drink takes its name from an old toast meaning “be well” or “good health”?
hint: Hot cider or ale with spices, and there’s a carol about taking it door to door.
funFact: Carolers went door to door singing and offering a sip from the bowl in exchange for gifts. Basically trick-or-treating with a punch bowl.

question: What German Christmas fruit bread, buried in powdered sugar, gets a giant parade-sized version at a festival in Dresden?
hint: Often has a log of marzipan inside, and it sounds like it was taken without asking.
funFact: Its shape and white sugar coating are said to represent the baby Jesus wrapped in swaddling clothes.

question: The gentle carol “Do You Hear What I Hear?” was written as a plea for peace during which Cold War crisis?
hint: It was written in October 1962, when the whole world held its breath.
funFact: The line “Pray for peace, people everywhere” reflects the fear of nuclear war that fall.

question: In White Christmas (1954), which comedian plays Bing Crosby's army buddy and song-and-dance partner?
hint: He played the daydreaming Walter Mitty in 1947.
funFact: Co-star Rosemary Clooney was George Clooney’s aunt. Talent runs in the family.

question: Netflix’s Oscar-nominated 2019 cartoon tells how a lazy postman named Jesper and a grumpy toymaker started the Santa legend. Title?
hint: A one-word title that’s also a common German first name.
funFact: It won the BAFTA for Best Animated Film plus seven Annie Awards. Not bad for a lazy-postman origin story.

question: In the 2024 action-comedy Red One, Dwayne Johnson and Chris Evans rescue a kidnapped Santa. Which actor plays Santa?
hint: Oscar winner for Whiplash, and the “We know a thing or two” insurance-ad guy.
funFact: Bonnie Hunt plays Mrs. Claus, and in this version the North Pole has its own security agency. Santa gets a bodyguard!

question: In “Winter Wonderland,” the couple builds a snowman in the meadow and pretends he is who?
hint: His last name is a color, and his job is performing weddings.
funFact: A later, kid-friendly version of the lyric turned him into a circus clown. Quite the career change!

question: Every December 23, Oaxaca, Mexico, holds a contest where artists carve entire nativity scenes out of which vegetable?
hint: A small red root veggie you usually find in a salad, grown supersized.
funFact: The Night of the Radishes began as a market gimmick to lure shoppers and became an official contest in 1897. Carvers use special oversized radishes.

question: Finland's Santa Claus is called Joulupukki. What does that name literally mean in English?
hint: Half “Christmas,” half a bearded farm animal with horns.
funFact: Long ago, costumed “Yule goats” went house to house rowdily demanding treats. Later the goat became the gift-giver, and in Finland the name stuck.

question: In Greek folklore, goblins called kallikantzaroi spend all year underground trying to saw through what, until Christmas interrupts them?
accept: The tree that holds up the Earth
The tree that holds up the world
The tree holding up the Earth
hint: Think lumberjacks, but the stakes are planet-sized.
funFact: They pop up to make mischief during the 12 days of Christmas. When they go back down, the tree has healed, and they have to start sawing all over again.

question: On December 7, Guatemalans “clean house” before Christmas by burning piles of junk, often topped with an effigy of whom?
hint: Horns, a pitchfork, a red suit... and definitely not coming down the chimney.
funFact: It's called La Quema del Diablo. Folk belief says he hides in the junk and under the furniture, so out goes the clutter and up goes the bonfire.

question: Spain's giant Christmas lottery, with winning numbers sung on live TV by schoolchildren, is nicknamed “El Gordo.” What does that mean in English?
hint: It describes your wallet after you win it.
funFact: Kids from Madrid's San Ildefonso school sing out the winning numbers in a sing-song chant that everyone in Spain knows by heart.

question: The Philippines celebrates the world's longest Christmas season. In which month do the carols and decorations traditionally kick off?
hint: It's the first of the so-called “ber” months.
funFact: Once the “ber months” arrive, the carols start and the celebrating runs until early January. That's more than four months of Christmas!

question: Every year since 1947, which country has sent London the giant Christmas tree in Trafalgar Square as a thank-you for help during World War II?
hint: Fjords, Vikings and a whole lot of very tall spruce trees.
funFact: It's usually a spruce over 20 meters tall and 50 to 60 years old, picked from the forest around Oslo. That's one well-traveled tree.
